market_context: United States; commercial honey and honey marketed as raw
title: Raw vs. pasteurized honey: what actually changes?

seo.title: Raw vs. pasteurized honey: what really changes
seo.meta_description: Heat can change honey enzymes, HMF, texture and crystallization. Learn what that means nutritionally—and what pasteurization does not change.
seo.search_intent: Understand the real differences between raw honey and honey that has been heated or pasteurized.

excerpt: Heating or pasteurizing honey can lower enzyme activity, raise HMF when treatment is intense, and delay crystallization by helping filtration and controlling yeasts. That does not make raw honey a radically different source of nutrition, and pasteurized honey is still not safe for children under one year because ordinary processing does not reliably destroy botulism spores.
content_html:
“Raw” and “pasteurized” sound as though they describe two opposite foods, but heating honey does not turn it into a different basic product. Both are still concentrated mixtures of sugars and water with much smaller amounts of enzymes, acids, minerals, aroma compounds, and polyphenols.

What changes depends on temperature and time together. Brief gentle warming to improve flow is not the same treatment as holding honey at a high temperature for a long period.

“Raw honey” does not tell you an exact processing history

In everyday U.S. marketing, raw generally means honey that has not been subjected to substantial heat and may have received less filtration. The label alone, however, does not tell you the precise extraction temperature, filtration method, or storage history.

That means two raw honeys can differ from each other, and two heated honeys can also have experienced very different time-temperature combinations. The meaningful question is what the processing actually did.

Heat first shows up in enzymes and quality markers

Honey naturally contains enzymes including diastase and invertase. They are heat-sensitive, so enzyme activity can fall as heating becomes more severe. At the same time, 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) can rise; HMF also increases during storage and is widely used as a marker of excessive heating or aging.

Those measurements matter for honey quality. They do not prove that a spoonful of raw honey delivers a clinically important dose of digestive enzymes that heated honey lacks. Honey enzymes are not essential nutrients with a dietary requirement.

What about antioxidants and micronutrients?

Thermal studies do not produce a simple all-or-nothing result. More severe heat can reduce some phenolic compounds and antioxidant measurements, while gentler processing causes smaller changes and results vary with floral source and analytical method.

The scale of the food still matters: a 20-g serving of honey provides roughly 16 g of sugars and about 61 calories. Its vitamin and mineral contribution is small. Choosing raw honey does not turn that serving into the nutritional equivalent of fruit, vegetables, or nuts.

Heating also solves practical processing problems

Warm honey is less viscous, easier to filter, and can have fewer viable yeasts that might contribute to fermentation when moisture is high enough. Heating can also dissolve existing glucose crystals and, together with fine filtration, help the product stay clear and liquid for longer.

That is why highly processed honey may crystallize more slowly. Crystallization itself is not spoilage; it is a physical change in which some glucose comes out of solution and forms crystals.

Pasteurized honey is still off-limits before age one

This is the most important safety distinction to get right. Children under 12 months should not be given honey because of the risk of infant botulism. Clostridium botulinum spores are highly resistant, and ordinary honey pasteurization is not designed to guarantee their destruction.

So a pasteurized label does not remove the infant rule. Raw honey is not uniquely subject to it; the recommendation applies to honey in general.

Choose for flavor and handling, not a health halo

If you value a particular floral aroma, minimal processing, or a texture that may crystallize sooner, raw honey may appeal to you. If you want a consistently clear, pourable product, heated and filtered honey may be more convenient.

Nutritionally, neither choice changes the central fact: both are primarily sugar-rich sweeteners. Flavor, source, and how much you use matter more in everyday eating than a blanket claim that raw honey is always nutritionally superior.

faq.question: Does raw honey have more nutrients than pasteurized honey?
faq.answer: It may retain more activity of some heat-sensitive enzymes and compounds, but a normal serving of either honey contains only small amounts of vitamins and minerals. Raw honey is not a radically different nutritional category.

faq.question: Does pasteurizing honey stop crystallization?
faq.answer: It can delay crystallization by dissolving existing crystals and assisting filtration, but it cannot guarantee that honey will never crystallize.

faq.question: Can a baby under one year have pasteurized honey?
faq.answer: No. The recommendation to avoid honey before 12 months applies to pasteurized honey too because ordinary processing does not reliably destroy the spores linked to infant botulism.
